sources.title: Load, Select, Filter, Clean and Group a CSV with pandas

steps.title: Install pandas and load orders.csv
steps.instructions: In an empty folder run `uv init .` and `uv add pandas`, download orders.csv from https://github.com/techwithtim/PanadasTutorial into it, then create main.py that imports pandas as pd, reads orders.csv with pd.read_csv and prints df. Run `uv run main.py` to see the DataFrame summary (40 rows x 9 columns).

targets.caption: Import pandas with the pd alias

explanations.topic: Installing pandas with pip or a uv virtual environment
Why pandas is imported as pd
DataFrame vs Series
CSV files and two-dimensional data
read_csv loads a file into a DataFrame
Automatic row indices

hints: First install pandas: run `uv init .` then `uv add pandas` (or `pip install pandas`).
Put orders.csv in the same folder as main.py so the relative path works.
In main.py: `import pandas as pd`, then `df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')` and `print(df)`.
Run it with `uv run main.py`. You should see a table ending with something like `[40 rows x 9 columns]`.
common_mistakes: Running `python main.py` outside the uv environment, causing ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'
orders.csv not in the folder you run from, causing FileNotFoundError
Typing `pd.readcsv` or `pd.read_CSV` instead of `pd.read_csv`
Saving the GitHub HTML page instead of the raw CSV, producing a parse error
Forgetting `print(df)`, so nothing appears when the script runs
steps.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')
print(df)

steps.title: Load the data in a notebook
steps.instructions: Create notebook.ipynb in the same folder, put `import pandas as pd` and `df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')` in cell 1 and run it (pick the project's Python kernel). Then run `print(df)` in a second cell.

targets.caption: Cell 1: import pandas and load the CSV

explanations.topic: Why use a Jupyter notebook instead of a .py file for pandas
Creating a notebook via Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P 'New Jupyter Notebook'
Python extension required for notebooks in VS Code
Cells run independently; data stays loaded between cells
Running, deleting cells and clearing outputs

hints: Open the command palette (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P) and choose 'New Jupyter Notebook', then save it as notebook.ipynb next to orders.csv.
In the first cell write import pandas as pd and df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv'), then click the run button and pick a Python kernel.
Add a new cell below and put print(df) in it; run only that cell — df is already loaded from the first.
If running fails, install the Python extension from the Extensions pane and make sure the chosen kernel has pandas installed.
common_mistakes: Saving the notebook in a different folder from orders.csv, causing FileNotFoundError.
Choosing a Python kernel/interpreter where pandas isn't installed (ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas').
Running the print(df) cell before running the read_csv cell, giving NameError: name 'df' is not defined.
Not having the VS Code Python extension installed, so 'New Jupyter Notebook' doesn't appear.
Typing pd.readcsv instead of pd.read_csv.
steps.run_command: Run cell 1 (select a Python kernel), then run cell 2
steps.code:
# cell 1
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')

# cell 2
print(df)

steps.title: Explore the DataFrame
steps.instructions: In new notebook cells run df.head(), df.tail(), df.info(), df.describe(), df.columns and df.index to inspect the data. Confirm info() reports the number of entries and columns.

explanations.topic: head() shows the first five rows
tail() shows the last five rows
info(): entries, columns and dtypes
Why text columns show as object dtype
describe() generates descriptive statistics
columns and index (RangeIndex start/stop/step)

hints: Make sure df is loaded from the previous step, then add a new cell for each call.
head() and tail() each show 5 rows; info() prints a summary including 'RangeIndex: N entries'.
columns and index are attributes, not methods: write df.columns and df.index without parentheses.
With orders.csv, info() should say 40 entries and 9 columns, and df.index should show RangeIndex(start=0, stop=40, step=1).
common_mistakes: Calling df.columns() or df.index() with parentheses, which raises a TypeError.
Running the cells before the cell that loads df, which causes a NameError.
Putting several calls in one cell and only seeing the last one's output (info() still prints).
Expecting describe() to show the text columns; by default it only summarizes numeric columns.
steps.run_command: Run each cell in the notebook
steps.code:
df.head()
df.tail()
df.info()
df.describe()
df.columns
df.index

steps.title: Select columns and rows
steps.instructions: Select one column with df['col'], several with df[['col1', 'col2']], and rows by position with df.iloc[0] and df.iloc[10]. Access a value with df.iloc[10]['col'].

targets.caption: Select two columns to get a new DataFrame
Select the row at position 10 with iloc

explanations.topic: Selecting a single column returns a pandas Series
Selecting a list of columns returns a DataFrame
iloc selects rows by integer position
Access a row's values by position or by column name

hints: Columns are selected with square brackets and the column name as a string. Run df.columns first to see the exact names.
To select several columns, pass a list inside the brackets: df[['Country', 'Product']]. That means double brackets.
Rows are selected by position with df.iloc[n]. Then index the resulting row by column name, for example df.iloc[10]['Country'].
Wrap a row in list(...) to see all of its values as a plain Python list.
common_mistakes: Using single brackets with two names, like df['Country', 'Product'], which raises a KeyError. You need a list: df[['Country', 'Product']].
Misspelling or miscapitalizing a column name ('country' instead of 'Country'), which causes a KeyError.
Writing df.iloc(10) with parentheses instead of square brackets df.iloc[10].
Expecting df.iloc[10] to be the 10th row, when it is actually the 11th because positions start at 0.
Using an iloc position beyond the number of rows, which raises an IndexError.
steps.code:
df.columns
df['Country']
len(df['Country'])
set(df['Country'])
df[['Country', 'Product']]
df.iloc[0]
df.iloc[10]
list(df.iloc[10])
df.iloc[10][0]
df.iloc[10]['Country']

steps.title: Filter rows with conditions
steps.instructions: Filter rows with boolean conditions like df[df['col'] == value], combine them with & and |, and compare numbers with >. Use .str.startswith() and ~df['col'].isin([...]) to filter text columns.

targets.caption: Filter rows with a boolean condition
Use string methods to filter text columns

explanations.topic: Boolean mask filtering df[df[col] == value]
Combining conditions with & and parentheses
Using | for or conditions
Numeric comparison filters (>, <, <=, !=)
.str string methods like startswith/endswith
isin and the ~ negation operator

hints: Put the condition inside df[...]: df[df['Category'] == 'Electronics'].
When combining conditions, wrap each one in parentheses and join them with a single & or |.
For text columns use .str methods, e.g. df['CustomerName'].str.startswith('A').
Use df['Country'].isin([...]) for a list of values and put ~ in front to exclude them.
common_mistakes: Filtering on the wrong column (e.g. 'Product' instead of 'Category') and getting an empty table
Using Python's `and`/`or` instead of & and |, which raises a ValueError about ambiguous truth value
Forgetting parentheses around each condition when combining with & or |
Calling .startswith directly on the Series without .str
Case mismatch in string filters, e.g. endswith('A') when names end in lowercase 'a'
Misspelling column names, causing a KeyError
steps.code:
df[df['Category'] == 'Electronics']
df[(df['Category'] == 'Electronics') & (df['Country'] == 'USA')]
df[(df['Category'] == 'Electronics') | (df['Country'] == 'USA')]
df[df['Quantity'] > 2]
df[df['CustomerName'].str.startswith('A')]
df[df['CustomerName'].str.endswith('a')]
df[df['Country'].isin(['USA', 'Sweden', 'Brazil'])]
df[~df['Country'].isin(['USA', 'Sweden', 'Brazil'])]

steps.title: Update and delete data
steps.instructions: In your notebook, update values with df.loc[condition, 'column'] = new_value and uppercase a text column with df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper(). Remove a row with df = df.drop(<index>) and confirm it is gone with df.tail().

targets.caption: Locate rows by a condition, then pick a column to update
Transform a whole column at once
Drop a row by its index label

explanations.topic: loc locates rows by label or condition, iloc by position
loc returns a DataFrame because several rows may match
df.loc[condition, column] = value updates the matching cells
Updating every USA row at once
Using .str.upper() to transform a whole column
drop removes a row by index; reassign the result to df

hints: Use df.loc[condition, 'ColumnName'] = new_value to update only the matching rows.
The condition looks like a filter: df['Country'] == 'USA'. Put it inside .loc[ ], followed by a comma and the column name.
For a whole column, use df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper().
df.drop(39) returns a new DataFrame. Write df = df.drop(39), then run df.tail() to confirm the row is gone.
common_mistakes: Using chained indexing such as df[df['Country']=='USA']['Country'] = ..., which raises SettingWithCopyWarning and doesn't update df.
Misspelling a column name (for example 'ProductName' instead of 'Product'), which silently creates a new column.
Writing .upper() instead of .str.upper() on a Series, which raises AttributeError.
Calling df.drop(39) without reassigning it to df, so the row is never actually removed.
Running drop(39) twice, which gives a KeyError because index 39 no longer exists.
Uppercasing first and then filtering for 'United States', which matches nothing because the values are now uppercase.
steps.code:
df.loc[df['CustomerName'] == 'Anna ...', 'Product'] = 'Tim'
df.loc[df['CustomerName'] == 'Anna ...']

df.loc[df['Country'] == 'USA', 'Country'] = 'United States'
df[df['Country'] == 'United States']

df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper()
df['Country']

df = df.drop(39)
df.tail()

steps.title: Clean missing values and rename
steps.instructions: Reload your CSV with pd.read_csv, then handle missing values with df.dropna() and df.fillna({...}, inplace=True). Rename a column with df.rename(columns={...}, inplace=True) and display df to confirm the new header.

targets.caption: Drop rows that contain missing values
Fill missing values in place instead of dropping them

explanations.topic: dropna removes rows with null/NA values
fillna fills missing values instead of dropping them
inplace=True modifies the existing DataFrame instead of returning a new one
Renaming columns with rename(columns=...)

hints: Reload the CSV first with pd.read_csv so you start from clean data.
df.dropna() returns a new DataFrame. To fill gaps instead, pass a dict of column -> value to df.fillna and add inplace=True.
Rename uses a mapping: df.rename(columns={'old': 'new'}, inplace=True). Then put df on its own line in a cell to display it.
Check that the column header in the printed table changed, for example 'OrderID' to 'Order ID'.
common_mistakes: Forgetting inplace=True, or not assigning the result, so the DataFrame never changes.
Calling df.rename({'OrderID': 'Order ID'}) without columns=, which renames index labels instead of the column.
Misspelling the column name in fillna or rename. rename silently does nothing, and fillna silently ignores the unknown key.
Expecting dropna to remove rows when the dataset has no missing values. Nothing changing is normal here.
Not reloading the CSV after earlier edits like df.drop, which leaves a messed-up DataFrame.
steps.code:
df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')
df.dropna()
df.fillna({'OrderID': 0}, inplace=True)
df.rename(columns={'OrderID': 'Order ID'}, inplace=True)
df

steps.title: Analyze, group and save
steps.instructions: Run value_counts() on a column, a groupby(...)[...].sum(), and sort_values(..., ascending=False). Save the result with df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False).

explanations.topic: value_counts counts each distinct value in a column
groupby works like SQL GROUP BY, aggregating with sum
sort_values with ascending=False sorts descending
to_csv saves the DataFrame; index=True/False controls writing the index

hints: Each operation goes in its own cell; the last expression in a cell is displayed.
Select the column before aggregating: df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum().
sort_values takes the column name plus ascending=False for highest first.
df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False) writes the file next to your notebook.
common_mistakes: Calling value_counts on the whole DataFrame instead of a column (df['Country'].value_counts()).
Forgetting parentheses on .sum(), which shows a method object instead of totals.
Using ascending=True (or omitting it) and getting the cheapest items first.
Column names not matching after the earlier rename step, causing a KeyError.
Omitting index=False and getting an extra unnamed index column in the saved CSV.
steps.code:
df['Country'].value_counts()

df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum()

df.sort_values('Price', ascending=False)

df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False)
